### Problem: Contains Duplicate II {#sec-hash-p3-b}

::: {.p-statement}
Given $a$ ($1 \le n \le 10^5$, $-10^9 \le a_i \le 10^9$) and $k$ ($0 \le k \le 10^5$), return whether there exist **distinct** indices $i \ne j$ with $a_i = a_j$ and $|i - j| \le k$.

Source: [LC 219 · Contains Duplicate II](https://leetcode.com/problems/contains-duplicate-ii/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Contains Duplicate (@sec-hash-p3-a) asks "have I seen this value *at all*?" — this one asks "have I seen it *recently*?", so the set graduates to a map of the single fact that answers recency: the **latest index** per value (@sec-hash-complement's table, now storing positions).
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Neighbourhood scan.** For each $i$, check $j \in (i, i+k]$: $O(nk)$ — $10^{10}$ at the limits, out.
2. **Last-seen map.** One pass: at $i$ with value $x$, if `last[x]` exists and $i - \text{last}[x] \le k$, done; always store `last[x] = i`. Storing only the *latest* index is enough: it has the smallest gap to the future. $O(n)$ expected.
3. (Equivalent window view: keep a set of the last $k$ elements, adding the new one and removing the one that falls out — the sliding window of @sec-sw, also $O(n)$.)

**Invariant.** Before position $i$, `last[x]` is the greatest index $< i$ with $a_{\text{last}[x]} = x$, for every $x$ seen.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Check each index's next k neighbours

::: {.form-next}
For every $i$, look ahead $k$ cells for an equal value. Exactly the statement, $O(nk)$ — with both up to $10^5$ that is a worst case of $10^{10}$, so the question is how to test "recently seen" without looking ahead at all.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def near_dup_brute(a, k):
    n = len(a)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, min(i + k + 1, n)):
            if a[i] == a[j]:
                return True
    return False
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

bool containsNearbyDuplicateBrute(vector<int>& a, int k) {
    int n = (int)a.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
        for (int j = i + 1; j < n && j <= i + k; ++j)
            if (a[i] == a[j]) return true;
    return false;
}
```
:::

#### Remember only the latest index

::: {.form-next}
Keep `last = {value: newest index}`. At $i$, the *newest* earlier copy is the only one that could be within $k$ — older copies are farther — so one lookup decides. Then overwrite: recency is what the invariant keeps.
:::

```{python}

V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-nearby-duplicate
def near_duplicate(a: list[int], k: int) -> bool:
    last = {}
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        j = last.get(x)
        if j is not None and i - j <= k:
            return True
        last[x] = i
    return False


for _ in range(1200):
    a = [random.randint(-4, 4) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 15))]
    k = random.randint(0, 6)
    assert near_duplicate(a, k) == near_dup_brute(a, k)

assert near_duplicate([1, 2, 3, 1], 3) is True        # the LC examples:
assert near_duplicate([1, 0, 1, 1], 1) is True        # gap of the last pair
assert near_duplicate([1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3], 2) is False # every copy 3 apart
assert near_duplicate([1, 2, 1], 2) is True           # the board sample
assert near_duplicate([7], 0) is False                # k = 0: indices distinct
print("near_duplicate OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <unordered_map>
using namespace std;

bool containsNearbyDuplicate(vector<int>& a, int k) {
    unordered_map<int, int> last;
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)a.size(); ++i) {
        auto it = last.find(a[i]);
        if (it != last.end() && i - it->second <= k) return true;
        last[a[i]] = i;                    // keep only the newest index
    }
    return false;
}
```
:::
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Check each index's next k neighbours** is $O(nk)$ worst case, $O(1)$ space. **Remember only the latest index** is $O(n)$ expected time and $O(n)$ space — and the *latest-is-enough* argument is the whole insight: one stored index per value answers every distance question. The window-set view is the same $O(n)$ with at most $k+1$ live set entries.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $k = 0$: no two *distinct* indices can be $0$ apart — always `False`; the code gets this free because $i - j \ge 1$.
- $k \ge n$: reduces to Contains Duplicate (@sec-hash-p3-a) — distance never binds.
- Negatives and $10^9$ magnitudes: pure hash territory; the C++ `int` keys stay safe because only indices are subtracted (@sec-arr-cost).
:::

::: {.practice}
- [CF 1702C · Train and Queries](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1702/C){rating="1100"} — keep the *first* and the *last* index of each value; each query compares two of them.
- [CSES 1141 · Playlist](https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1141) — the latest-index map decides how far the left edge of a window must jump.
:::
